question: Which question decides whether a Najdorf knight jump, ...Nxe4 or ...Rxc3 works, and how do you test it by counting before you play it? (The Poisoned Pawn is decided by other things, and the lesson says so.)
outcomes: Counts the attackers and defenders of e4 after a knight jump from c3 and says when ...Nxe4 wins a pawn
Explains why Nd5 works in the English Attack (the f3 pawn guards e4, the d6 pawn blocks the queen) and why ...Nxd5 then fails
Steps through the Poisoned Pawn line and names the moves the engine rates best and the alternatives it also accepts, with the engine evidence
Finds ...Nxe4 after ...Rxc3 bxc3 and says why it is the only move
Recognises tempting grabs that fail (...Nxe4 against 6.Be2 and 6.Bg5) and says why

steps.chapter: Count the guard before the jump

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** Several Najdorf shots (a knight jump, ...Nxe4, a rook sacrifice on c3) turn on one question: which piece guards the key square, and what happens when it moves or is taken? Ask it first and test it by counting. The Poisoned Pawn is decided by other things (queen safety, development), and its chapter says so. [V] checked here, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis.

steps.text: **The idea: a guard that leaves.** A defended pawn is safe only while the defender stays. If you move the defender with a threat of your own, the pawn can still be taken. Before any knight jump, count the attackers and defenders of the squares the piece leaves behind. Conditions: the pawn is attacked by a black piece, and White's move does not take or threaten something bigger.

steps.text: **When Nd5 works: the English Attack.** With the pawn on f3, e4 stays guarded when the knight leaves c3. White can then play Nd5, offer to trade it for the bishop on e6 or the knight on f6, and take a pawn on d5 that squeezes Black. In our master file Nd5 was played 163 times in this position.

steps.text: **What Nd5 does [I].** It trades one of Black's pieces for a knight, and the recapture on d5 leaves White with a pawn that restricts the e6 and c6 squares. It works because the f3 pawn guards e4. Remove the f3 pawn and the verdict changes (you saw it). The d6 pawn matters in this one recapture: it stops Black's queen from defending a knight on d5. [I] [H] The trade is attractive because the structure gets harder for Black to unlock.

**The Poisoned Pawn.** After 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 Black's queen can go to b6. White's bishop has left c1, so b2 has no guard; White keeps the queen on the d-file to defend the d4 knight and offers the pawn as bait. In our master file 7.f4 was played 711 times and 7...Qb6 244 times. This chapter tests whether the pawn is really poisoned.

steps.text: **A rook for a knight and a pawn?** In the e5 structure the knight on c3 guards e4 and d5. A black rook on the open c-file attacks it. If the rook takes, the recapture bxc3 leaves e4 without a guard, the same fact as in the first chapter. This is a sacrifice, so test it before you trust it.

steps.text: **Why it holds, and when it does not [I].** The sacrifice works because the recapture bxc3 removes the knight and leaves e4 with no guard, while the knight on f6 already attacks it. If a second white piece guarded e4, for example a bishop on d3, then ...Nxe4 would lose a piece. So count the guards of e4 first, then offer the rook. [H] The engine treats the sacrifice as one of several equal choices, so it is a way to unbalance the game, not a necessity.

**Tempting grabs that fail.** The knight on f6 attacks e4 on every move of the opening. The pawn can be taken when its guard is gone (chapter 1). When the guard is still there, the grab loses a piece. Two examples with different reasons.

steps.text: **Typical mistakes and where they come from [I].** (1) Moving the guard of a pawn without a bigger threat. (2) Grabbing a pawn that is still guarded. (3) Sacrificing a rook without counting what the recapture leaves behind. All three are the same error: not asking which piece guards the key square. Our data cannot say how often these errors occur; they are what the boards above show.

**Recap.** Count the guards of the key square before you jump, grab or sacrifice. A knight jump from c3 leaves e4 loose unless f3, a bishop or another piece guards it. Nd5 works in the English Attack because f3 holds e4. ...Rxc3 works because it removes the guard of e4. Grabs fail while the guard stands. The Poisoned Pawn is not a guard count: queen escape squares and development decide it, and draws are common in our data.
